agents.description: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions.

# The History of the Printing Press

## Before Print

For most of human history, the reproduction of text was a matter of hands and patience. Scribes in monasteries, government offices, and merchant houses copied manuscripts letter by letter, a process so slow that a single Bible could take a skilled copyist the better part of a year to complete. Books were consequently rare and expensive, the property of institutions and the wealthy rather than ordinary people. Literacy itself was constrained by this scarcity: there was little incentive to learn to read when reading material was so difficult to obtain.

Printing technology existed before Johannes Gutenberg, though not in the form that would reshape Europe. In China, woodblock printing had been used since at least the seventh century, and Bi Sheng developed a movable type system using fired clay characters around 1040. Korea advanced this further, casting movable type in metal by the thirteenth century and producing, in 1377, the Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with metal movable type. These innovations were significant, but the nature of Chinese and Korean writing systems, which relied on thousands of distinct characters, limited the practical advantage of movable type over block printing. A printer needed to maintain an enormous inventory of characters, and the labor savings compared to skilled woodblock carving were less dramatic than they would prove to be in an alphabetic language.
